'Record a goose sighting' is a made-up government service, filled with accessibility issues. Your task is to find them all!

To help find the issues, install Accessibility Insights for Web in Microsoft Edge or Google Chrome. Start with Fast Pass, then use Tab stops and the manual checks to find what automated checks cannot. You'll also need to try to complete the exercise using just your keyboard. Read the tips on what to look for and how to record your findings.

Accessibility issues start on the next page. Good luck!

Continue

Accessibility issues in 'Record a goose sighting'

Here is the answer sheet for the 'Record a goose sighting' accessibility testing exercise. There are 19 issues in total.

Some of these issues would not be WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) 2.1 failures. But, they could present issues to users with access needs, and WCAG compliance doesn't neccessarily mean that something is accessible.

Many of these problems are missed by automated tools and by a quick keyboard check. See which issues need manual testing and why.

Pages

Start page

Two h1 tags
It is good practice to have only one h1 tag. A h1 tag specifies what the top level heading is for the entire page. It used to be permissible to have another h1 tag nested within a section element, but this was depracated in HTML 5.1. This isn't a WCAG 2.1 failure.
Altered tab order on side menu
The tab order is a bit random, when you're tabbing through the list of links on the right-hand side of the page. This is unpredictable, and a bit disorienting. Whilst it's not a huge issue in this scenario, if the links were further apart on the page, or spread out more, it could cause issues for users who use a screen magnifier or browser zoom. They might not be able to tell where focus is gone, and have to hunt from it, or might have had their screen view dragged across the page as it's following focus (depending on how they've configured their assistive technologies).
Link opens in new tab
Opening a link in a new tab can be appropriate if you tell the user in advance that it's going to happen. This can be done with either with content in the link text or with an icon that has appropriate alternative text. In this case, neither of these techniques have been used. This is an issue because the user may not be aware the the new tab or windows has opened. They then can't use the back button on the keyboard to navigate to where they were, as a new tab history has been opened.
Undescriptive link text
Screen reader users can view links out of context through a links menu. This can be quicker to skim through. If link text doesn't make sense out of context, it would be unusable when viewed this way. The 'More' link on the start page doesn't make any sense out of context - we can infer it means more about geese by seeing that it is in a section titled 'Information about Geese'. This isn't a failure against WCAG 2.1 Level AA criteria but is really useful to do.
Poor focus styling on link
If the focus state style doesn't have a high enough contrast and it can be really hard to tell where focus is. This particularly effects people who have a sight impairement. In this instance, this issue can be fixed by adding the appropriate Design System link class.
Image alternative is a file name
The start-page illustration has alt="goose-illustration.svg". A screen reader user hears the file name rather than a description of the goose beside the pond. A non-empty alternative passes automated checks, but 1.1.1 requires the alternative to be equivalent to the image.

Do you like geese page

Missing page title
Some screen readers (like JAWS) read the page title out when a page loads. On this page, there is no title, which means a screen reader user is missing context. An example of a possible page title would be the page question, followed by the service name, and followed by whatever it's hosted on - so 'Do you like geese - Recording a goose sighting - GOV.UK', if it were on GOV.UK.
No legend on the radio button
We can visually tell that the buttons relate to the main heading by looking at the page. But, the question isn't linked up to the element in a way that makes sense for users who can't see. For radio buttons and checkboxes, it's important to have a legend element. The fix would be making sure the 'h1' is inside the 'legend', as per the Design System pattern.
Continue button isn’t keyboard focusable
You can still get past this page by pressing enter when on the radio buttons, but a user might not know this. They might (understandably) expect that the only way to progress is by submitting enter, and so feel trapped and abandon the service at this point. All interactive elements must be usabled with the keyboard. The fix would be removing the tabindex="-1".
Insufficient colour contrast of the form hint
The colour contrast is way too low for the form hint text. In the Design System, it's a darker grey, which does have a sufficient colour contrast ratio. Respecting the out-of-the-box colours and not overriding them here would fix this issue.

What type of goose did you see

Wrong page title
Some screen readers (like JAWS) read the page title out when a page loads. On this page, the page title is 'Boop - Record a goose sighting', which tells the screen reader user nothing about what's on the page. A better format would be the page question, followed by the service name, and followed by whatever it's hosted on - so 'What type of goose did you see - Recording a goose sighting - GOV.UK', if it were on GOV.UK.
Visually hidden item you can tab onto
There is a ghost goose hidden on the page! There is some hidden text on the page, that can be tabbed to. Whilst this isn't a particularly realistic example of this issue, sometimes inputs can get hidden off screen. It can be confusing for keyboard users who are tabbing through the screen, because the focus disappears, and you end up not being entirely sure where or when it's going to reappear, or what would happen if you tried to select the element you were on. If something has focus, it's best that it becomes visible, at least for the duration of it having focus. In many cases think whether there is value for other users by having the content visible at all times.
Placeholder text
Placeholder text disappears when you start to type. This can be confusing, and if you struggle to remember things, you might then need to delete what you've typed in to remind yourself of what was there, in case it was important. It's best to include information like hints outside of the form field, where it can be seen at all times. This is essential if the placeholder text includes important formatting information.

When did you see the goose

No issues on this page!

Sometimes, when you've found issues on other pages, you expect every page to have issues, and you spend a long time looking. However sometimes, some pages don't have issues, and if the basic tests pass, the best use of time is to move on.

Check your answers

Change link - hidden text is incorrect
We talked earlier about links needing to make sense out of context. In this component from the Design System, given the change link is just across from the question, it would look weird to have that visually included in the link. But, we can visually hide text - and that's what is normally done here. A sighted user would see 'change', but a screen reader user would hear 'change what type of goose did you see'. However, it's been configured incorrectly here - and random food items have been put in the visually hidden text, instead of proper text.
Incorrect heading level hierarchy
The heading hierarchy is currently h1 > h3. The 'goose details' heading should be a h2, as it is a direct descendant of the h1. This is an issue because screen reader users can pull all of the headings out into one summary list, as a quick way of skim reading through what is on the page. If the ordering is incorrect like this, it can be hard to interpret when viewed in this way. When heading levels are not included users might also spend time looking for the heading thinking they are missing something.

End page

Use of capital letters
Text that is in all capital letters loses its shape. This can make it harder for some people with dyslexia to read. Unless absolutely necessary (like it is in a reference number), it's best to avoid writing words entirely in capital letters.
Justified text
Justified text forces words and letters to space out a little more than they normally would. This distorts the overall sentence shape a little. This justifying and centering content like this can make it harder to read for some people with dyslexia. The fix would be removing the styling that makes it justify, and allowing it to flow normally. This isn't a failure against WCAG 2.1 Level AA criteria but is really useful to do.
No alternative content for the gif
This gif shows a happy goose celebrating knowledge about geese being shared with the world. This information isn't captured in any other medium like text on the page though, so descriptive alt text needs to be added here. If an img element doesn't have an alt attribute then the href of the image may be read out by screen readers. There is a handy alt decision tree by W3C on how to decide how to write alt text, which is worth a look at.
Animation cannot be stopped.
Moving content such as the happy goose can be a severe distraction for people with conditions such as attention deficit disorders, making it difficult to use the rest of the page. It should run no longer than 5 seconds or be able to be paused or hidden by the users.

Extra keyboard practice

The keyboard focus practice page is not one of the six pages above. It deliberately contains focus failures that an Accessibility Insights Fast Pass does not report:

  • A link with no visible focus indicator. Tab to it and watch the focus disappear.
  • A button with a focus outline that has almost no contrast against the page. Tab to it and compare the outline colour with the background.
  • A link covered by a fixed banner. Tab to it and check whether you can see the focused element or its indicator.

These are manual checks: focus visibility, focus appearance and focus not being obscured are not decided by the axe-based Fast Pass. Use Tab stops and the keyboard, then record what you observed.

Inapplicable cases

These pages contain no eligible target for the named rule. “Inapplicable” is an ACT outcome, not a scanner that failed to run.

  • No buttons — rule 97a4e1 inapplicable.
  • No images — rule 23a2a8 inapplicable.

User-preference scenarios

Manual rendering comparisons. These are not ACT fixtures and do not establish conformance.

  • Reduced motion — one animation respects the preference, one ignores it.
  • Forced colours — an outline survives; a background-image focus cue does not.
  • Text spacing and reflow — increased spacing at 320 CSS pixels.

Dynamic, frame and interaction tests

Deterministic states that exercise asynchronous updates, node replacement, nested shadow roots, same-origin frames and disclosure interactions.

  • React: name supplied after mount — stable ?state=async, ready marker async-ready.
  • React: target node replaced — stable ?state=replaced, explicit replace action.
  • Vue: reactive name after mount — stable ?state=async.
  • Paca: nested open shadow roots — target inside a shadow root inside another shadow root.
  • Single frame, nested frame and two frames — same-origin targets in different browsing contexts.
  • Reveal an unnamed control — the target is absent until the disclosure opens.

Correlation experiments

Deliberate fixtures for testing target identity, duplicate detection and multiple rules on one element. These are not isolated single-target ACT cases.

  • Two distinct image failures — two failing images with the same class and a passing control; three declared targets.
  • One image, one failure — the simplest shared-target case, linked to the original confirmation page example.
  • Two rules on one target — one button, two independent ACT rule failures.
  • Repeated controls — three equivalent failures and two passing controls, each a separate target.

Interpreting results

Examples where a tool flags something that is not a WCAG failure, and examples that pass a tool but fail review.

  • Interpreting tool results — ten cases covering best practice versus failure, incomplete results, context-dependent link text, inaccurate alternatives, visual order and status messages.

Catalogue

Browse all fixtures by ACT rule, expected outcome, framework, category, context, interaction and review status. The catalogue is generated from the manifest; filters add to the static category lists and do not replace them.

What automation misses

Automated tools catch some of the issues in this exercise. Most of them need a person using the page in a particular way.

This exercise describes 19 issues. Automated checks catch 4 of them. The other 15 need manual checks, judgement, or both.

Detection was assessed with the axe-core 4.14 rules used by Accessibility Insights for Web Fast Pass, plus manual review. Tools change, and a rule appearing or disappearing is not a statement about WCAG conformance.

Text spacing and reflow

Apply increased text spacing and a 320 CSS-pixel viewport. The page should not clip or scroll horizontally. This is a manual rendering test, not an ACT fixture.

A longer passage

Accessibility testing is not a single scan. A page can have a complete heading outline, a valid document language and named controls, and still be difficult to use when text is enlarged, spacing is increased or the viewport is narrow. Read this passage at 200% zoom and again at 320 CSS pixels.

Check that no text is cut off, that words do not overlap, and that controls remain large enough to use. The page may wrap into a single column; that is expected. Horizontal scrolling is the signal to investigate.

  • Line height at least 1.5 times the font size.
  • Paragraph spacing at least twice the font size.
  • Letter spacing at least 0.12 times the font size.
  • Word spacing at least 0.16 times the font size.

Interpreting tool results

These are deliberate examples. Some trigger a tool rule without being a WCAG failure; others pass a tool but need human review. The surrounding laboratory interface is intended to be usable.

1. A best-practice finding, not a WCAG failure

Section heading

Subheading that skips a level
Tool output and review conclusion
Tool outputaxe reports heading-order as a best-practice rule.
Review conclusionNot a WCAG 2.1 AA failure, but the structure is harder to skim. Fix it.
WhyHeading order is useful for navigation, but WCAG does not require a specific level sequence.

2. A finding the tool cannot decide

Dark text on a light gradient. The measured colours pass 4.5:1, but the background is an image so automation cannot be certain.

Tool output and review conclusion
Tool outputaxe returns color-contrast as incomplete, not a violation.
Review conclusionMeasure the actual rendered colours. Do not report an incomplete check as a failure or a pass.
WhyThe tool cannot resolve a background image; a person can.

3. A tool pass that is correct: decorative image

Tool output and review conclusion

4. A tool pass that fails review: unhelpful alternative

Tool output and review conclusion

5. A tool pass that fails review: invisible focus

A link whose focus indicator has been removed
Tool output and review conclusion
Tool outputNo automated finding for focus visibility.
Review conclusion2.4.7 failure. Keyboard users cannot tell where focus is.
WhyFocus visibility is a rendering outcome, not a rule most scanners test.

6. A tool pass that needs review: hidden instruction

Use at least three characters.

Tool output and review conclusion
Tool outputNo automated finding: the input has a label and a description.
Review conclusionManual concern. Sighted users never see the instruction; a screen reader user may only hear it.
WhyThe description is present in the accessibility tree but hidden visually.

7. A tool pass that depends on context: uninformative link text

Read more

Tool output and review conclusion
Tool outputNo link-name finding: the link has non-empty text.
Review conclusionContext-dependent, not automatically a 2.4.4 failure. In a links list, "Read more" has no determinable purpose. If the surrounding sentence names the destination, it can pass.
WhyThe rule checks that a name exists. It cannot decide whether the name identifies the destination in every context.
How to test
  1. Open the links list in a screen reader, or read the link without its surrounding sentence.
  2. Ask: can you name the destination from the link text alone?
  3. Repeat with the surrounding paragraph present. Record both observations; do not change the verdict to "failure" unless the purpose is unavailable in every realistic context.

8. A tool pass that fails review: an inaccurate image alternative

Tool output and review conclusion
Tool outputNo image-alt finding: an alternative attribute is present.
Review conclusion1.1.1 failure. The alternative does not describe the image.
WhyAutomation checks for a non-empty alternative, not whether it is equivalent to the image's purpose.
How to test
  1. Open the images list in a screen reader and listen to the alternative.
  2. Compare it with the visible image and with the image's role in the page.
  3. Record the heard alternative and why it is or is not equivalent.

9. A tool pass that needs a keyboard: visual order differs from DOM order

First item in the DOM Second item in the DOM
Tool output and review conclusion
Tool outputNo automated finding: both links have names and valid targets.
Review conclusionPotential 1.3.2 / 2.4.3 issue, context-dependent. The second item appears first visually, but Tab follows DOM order. If the sequence carries meaning, the mismatch is a failure.
WhyCSS order and flex-direction change rendering without changing DOM or focus order.
How to test
  1. Tab from the address bar through the two links and record the order.
  2. Compare it with the left-to-right visual order.
  3. At 320 px and 200% zoom, check the order again.
  4. Decide whether reading the content in the keyboard order changes its meaning.

10. A tool pass that needs a listener: an uninformative status message

No update

Tool output and review conclusion
Tool outputNo automated finding: the status region is valid and the button has a name.
Review conclusionUsability concern, not a 4.1.3 failure by itself. The message is announced, but "Updated" does not say what changed or whether the action succeeded.
WhyStatus-message rules can confirm that a live region exists; they do not judge whether the announcement is useful.
How to test
  1. With a screen reader running, activate the button.
  2. Listen to the announcement without looking at the screen.
  3. Record whether you can tell what changed and whether the action succeeded.
